Problem Statement  
Scaling frontend applications often hits a wall when monolithic architectures become unwieldy. Teams struggle with maintainability, performance bottlenecks, and the complexity of integrating third-party services. A recent project faced this when a legacy codebase grew to 200,000+ lines, with duplicated UI components and a bloated bundle size exceeding 5MB. The result? Slow load times, fragmented team workflows, and a fragile deployment pipeline.  

Failed Approaches  
Early attempts to refactor involved splitting components into smaller modules, but without a cohesive strategy, this led to duplicated logic and inconsistent state handling. One team even tried a microfrontends approach using Iframe-based isolation, which introduced latency and broke shared authentication flows. Another attempt to adopt a global state manager like Redux resulted in a tangled web of action creators and reducer files, making the codebase harder to debug. These solutions felt like temporary fixes rather than systemic improvements.  

Working Solution  
The breakthrough came by embracing a modular, tree-shakeable architecture with Next.js 13’s App Router. We organized the codebase into domain-specific folders, each housing components, hooks, and API routes. TypeScript enforced strict type safety across shared utilities, while GraphQL abstracted data fetching, reducing redundant HTTP calls. For performance, we leveraged Next.js’ built-in ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration) and code splitting to keep initial load times under 2 seconds. Testing became streamlined with Jest and Cypress, ensuring changes didn’t break existing flows. Stakeholder alignment was key—weekly syncs with backend teams ensured API design matched frontend needs, avoiding redundant work.  

Why It Works  
This approach decouples UI logic from data concerns, making the codebase easier to scale. GraphQL’s query batching reduced network overhead, while TypeScript’s type inference minimized runtime errors. The modular structure also allowed teams to work independently on features without stepping on each other’s toes. By prioritizing performance from the start—using Lighthouse to track metrics—we achieved a 40% improvement in Time to Interactive. The result? A maintainable codebase that’s 3x faster to iterate on, with clear ownership of components and APIs.  

Future Work  
Next steps include adopting WebAssembly for computationally heavy tasks and exploring server components for even tighter client-server integration. We’re also evaluating a hybrid approach to microfrontends, using custom routing to balance modularity with shared state. The goal remains: build systems that scale with the business, not against it.
